summary: Describes the format of a request to a Time Stamping Authority and of its response, and sets security requirements for how a TSA handles requests.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3161 defines a request for a trusted timestamp and the signed response. The requester sends a fingerprint of its data, so the authority can certify a time without receiving the data itself.

questions: how to get a trusted timestamp
what is a time stamping authority
subtitle: A signed token proves that a data fingerprint existed before a stated time.

tldr.problem: A signature, record or other datum may need evidence that it existed before a particular time, such as before a signing certificate was revoked.
tldr.mechanism: A requester sends a hash of the datum to a Time Stamping Authority. The authority returns a signed token containing that hash, a time and a unique serial number.
tldr.outcome: A requester can verify the token without sending the original data to the authority. RFC 3161 is updated by RFC 5816.

today: RFC 3161 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2001. It has been updated by RFC 5816.

sections.title: What a Time Stamp Establishes
sections.content:
A Time Stamping Authority (TSA) provides evidence that a datum existed before a particular time. It may operate as a trusted third party or serve an organization's internal needs. One use is to check whether a digital signature was made before the signer's certificate was revoked.

The RFC does not set the TSA's complete operating policy. A TSA is expected to publish its practices, and clients should use it only if those practices meet their needs. The TSA must use a trustworthy time source and assign each token a unique integer.
sections.plainLanguage: A timestamp can show that data existed by the time named in a signed token. The client still needs to decide whether it trusts the authority's published policies.

sections.title: What the TSA Signs
sections.content:
The TSA stamps only a data imprint: a hash of the submitted datum, together with the identifier of the hash algorithm. It checks that the hash length fits that algorithm, but does not inspect the imprint or include the requester's identity in the token.

Each token is signed with a key reserved for timestamping. The TSA's certificate must identify that purpose with the critical id-kp-timeStamping extended key usage. The token also identifies the TSA policy under which it was created.
sections.plainLanguage: The authority receives a hash rather than the original data. It signs the hash with a key reserved for creating time-stamp tokens.

sections.title: Request, Response and Token
sections.content:
A request contains version v1 and a message imprint. It may also include a requested policy, a nonce, a request for the TSA certificate and extensions. If the requester sends a nonce, the response must return the same value. This lets the requester check that the response belongs to its request.

The response contains a status and may contain a TimeStampToken. Status granted (0) or grantedWithMods (1) requires a token; other status values do not include one. The token is signed data containing the policy, imprint, serial number and generation time, plus optional fields such as accuracy.
sections.plainLanguage: The requester sends the hash and may add a random nonce. The response reports success or failure and, on success, carries the TSA's signed token.

sections.title: How a Requester Checks a Token
sections.content:
The requester checks the response status, the token fields and the TSA's signature. It confirms that the token contains the requested data imprint, hash algorithm and TSA certificate identifier. If any required check fails, the requester rejects the token.

The requester also checks timeliness using a trusted local time reference or the nonce returned by the TSA. It SHOULD check whether the TSA certificate has been revoked and whether the TSA policy is acceptable for the application.
sections.plainLanguage: The requester verifies the signature and checks that the token refers to its own data fingerprint. It also checks the time and whether the TSA's certificate and policy are acceptable.

sections.title: Ways to Carry the Messages
sections.content:
The RFC does not require one transport. It describes optional e-mail, file, TCP and HTTP methods. E-mail uses the MIME types application/timestamp-query and application/timestamp-reply; files contain the DER encoding of one message.

The TCP method uses port 318 and can return a polling reference when a result is not ready. HTTP carries the encoded request and response using the same query and reply media types. A server must return a valid response or an HTTP error for a valid request.
sections.plainLanguage: The timestamp messages can travel by e-mail, files, TCP or HTTP. The TCP method also supports polling when the TSA needs more time.

sections.title: Protecting Trust in Tokens
sections.content:
If a TSA stops operating without a key compromise, its certificate is revoked; the revocation reason affects whether earlier tokens remain valid. If its private key is compromised, tokens signed with that key can no longer be trusted. The RFC describes audit records and tokens from two TSAs as possible ways to distinguish genuine tokens from backdated ones.

A token can reveal that two requests used the same data and hash algorithm because their imprints match. The RFC RECOMMENDS a nonce to detect replays. A requester relying only on a nonce and no local clock should treat an excessively delayed response as suspect.
sections.plainLanguage: A timestamp depends on keeping the TSA's signing key trustworthy. Nonces help detect replayed responses, while a compromised key can undermine tokens made with it.
